rewrites.title: Acute degron-based AP-1 depletion at different time points
rewrites.description: Use dTAG/auxin-inducible degradation of FOS, JUN, or a dominant-negative (A-FOS) to remove AP-1 either during the priming stimulus or after it has ended. If depleting AP-1 after priming erases the enhanced secondary response, AP-1 is needed to maintain memory; if only depletion during priming matters, it is needed for initiation but not maintenance.

rewrites.title: Single-cell multiome and lineage tracing of memory states
rewrites.description: Perform single-cell RNA plus ATAC on stimulated and naive populations over time, combined with heritable barcodes or live reporters of AP-1 activity. This reveals whether memory is carried by cell-autonomous states inherited through divisions, and whether it correlates with prior AP-1 dynamics in individual cells.

rewrites.title: Acute degradation to separate initiation from maintenance
rewrites.description: Tag endogenous AP-1 factors (JUN, FOSL, BATF) with a degron and deplete them either during the priming stimulus or only after the memory state has formed. If memory sites (ChIP/CUT&RUN, ATAC, H3K27ac) persist and the enhanced response remains after AP-1 loss at later times, AP-1 is only an initiator. If memory decays, AP-1 is required for maintenance.

rewrites.title: Longitudinal chromatin accessibility and AP-1 binding profiling
rewrites.description: Use ATAC-seq, CUT&RUN/CUT&Tag for FOS/JUN family members, and H3K27ac at time points before, during, and long after the stimulus. Test whether AP-1-dependent enhancers stay open or primed after AP-1 levels return to baseline, and whether motif-containing sites show persistent accessibility.

rewrites.title: Reversibility and decay kinetics of AP-1 memory
rewrites.description: Track AP-1 binding (CUT&RUN), accessibility and target transcription at repeated time points after the stimulus ends, and fit decay half-lives. Compare them with the cell division number, using synchronized or arrested cells to separate passive dilution from active maintenance, to test whether the memory is stable or decays over time.

rewrites.title: Longitudinal ATAC-seq/CUT&RUN of AP-1 occupancy after transient stimulus
rewrites.description: Profile chromatin accessibility and FOS/JUN binding before, during, and long after a transient stimulus (e.g., injury, inflammation, or stress) to test whether AP-1-dependent accessible sites persist after the stimulus is withdrawn and the AP-1 protein itself has returned to baseline.

rewrites.title: Enhancer-specific causal perturbation of AP-1 motifs
rewrites.description: Use CRISPR base editing or saturation mutagenesis of AP-1 motifs at primed enhancers, together with dCas9-KRAB or dCas9-based eviction, applied before or after priming. Measure whether the motif is required for establishing the open state, for keeping it, and for faster re-induction of the linked gene. Compare with other motifs to show that the memory is attributable to AP-1 sites specifically.

rewrites.title: Transient stimulus with long-term chromatin accessibility tracking
rewrites.description: Give cells a brief pulse of a stimulus that activates AP-1 (e.g., TPA, a growth factor, or an inflammatory cue). Then run time-resolved ATAC-seq and CUT&RUN for AP-1 factors (FOS, JUN) and histone marks (H3K27ac, H3K4me1) over days to weeks after the signal is removed. Memory predicts that a subset of AP-1 motif-containing enhancers stays open or marked after AP-1 itself returns to baseline.

rewrites.title: Live-cell reporters of AP-1 activity dynamics
rewrites.description: Track AP-1 activity using fluorescent reporters or tagged FOS/JUN in single cells over days and across divisions to measure persistence, bistability, and positive feedback (e.g., c-Jun autoregulation), and relate past activity history to current state.

rewrites.title: Chromatin-state coupling of AP-1 with BAF and histone marks, plus in vivo test
rewrites.description: Test whether AP-1 recruits BAF remodelers and deposits H3K27ac or H3K4me1 that persist, using BRG1 inhibition, ChIP/CUT&Tag and sequential perturbation. Then check in vivo, for example in skin or after inflammation, whether tissue cells retain AP-1-dependent accessible regions weeks after injury and respond faster on re-challenge.

rewrites.title: Site-specific perturbation of AP-1 motifs at memory enhancers
rewrites.description: Use CRISPR base editing or motif deletion at individual AP-1 sites, plus dCas9-based tethering of AP-1 or chromatin remodelers (e.g., BAF), to test whether single sites are necessary and sufficient for retained accessibility and faster re-induction. A few key sites that guide the larger accessibility pattern should show disproportionate effects, which can be tested by ranking sites by effect size.

rewrites.title: Primed-versus-naive re-stimulation response with motif-site mutagenesis
rewrites.description: Measure the transcriptional response (nascent RNA, PRO-seq) to a second stimulus in primed and naive cells, and identify the genes with enhanced responses. Then use CRISPR to mutate or dCas9-block the AP-1 motifs at selected enhancers to test whether those sites are necessary for the enhanced response. Add a reporter-based test of whether the primed state is cis-encoded.

rewrites.title: Transient stimulus with delayed re-challenge
rewrites.description: Expose cells to a defined, transient AP-1-activating stimulus (e.g., TPA, TNF, or injury signal), let AP-1 activity return to baseline, then re-stimulate days to weeks later. Compare transcriptional output (RNA-seq, nascent RNA) and kinetics against naive cells to test for primed or enhanced responses.

rewrites.title: Longitudinal ATAC-seq/CUT&RUN of AP-1 occupancy after transient stimulus
rewrites.description: Profile chromatin accessibility and AP-1 (FOS/JUN) binding at timepoints during and long after a transient stimulus (e.g., wounding, inflammation, stress) to see whether AP-1-dependent accessible sites persist after the signal and AP-1 levels have returned to baseline.

rewrites.title: Causal necessity/sufficiency tests with acute degradation and optogenetic pulses
rewrites.description: Use degron-tagged FOS/JUN or a dominant-negative (A-FOS) at different times (during priming, during the memory window, or at recall) to ask whether AP-1 is needed to establish versus maintain the memory. Pair this with optogenetic or chemogenetic AP-1 pulses of varied duration, amplitude and frequency to map the input–memory function, and test whether sufficiency alone can write the state.

rewrites.title: Single-cell lineage-linked memory tracing
rewrites.description: Use live reporters of AP-1 activity (FOS promoter or AP-1 response element reporters) with barcoded lineage tracing, and record each cell's history of AP-1 activity, then ask whether sister cells inherit similar states and similar future responsiveness. Co-measure single-cell multiome (RNA and ATAC) to test whether AP-1 history predicts the chromatin state better than the current signal does.

rewrites.title: Acute AP-1 degradation after priming (degron/dominant-negative)
rewrites.description: Use inducible degradation (dTAG/AID) or dominant-negative A-FOS at different times: during priming versus after the stimulus has ended. If the memory response persists when AP-1 is removed after priming, AP-1 is only an initiator. If it is lost, AP-1 is needed to maintain memory.

rewrites.title: Motif-level perturbation and feedback-loop modeling
rewrites.description: Edit AP-1 motifs at candidate enhancers with CRISPR base editing, or run a massively parallel reporter assay, to test whether memory is locus-intrinsic. In parallel, build a dynamical model with AP-1 positive autoregulation (c-Jun autoinduction) and chromatin feedback, fit it to the data, and test whether it predicts when memory is stable, using inhibition of feedback components as the falsification step.

rewrites.title: Acute degradation of AP-1 after the priming phase
rewrites.description: Use a degron (dTAG/auxin) or a dominant-negative such as A-Fos to remove AP-1 either during priming or only after it, then test whether the primed state persists. If the memory survives AP-1 loss after priming, AP-1 acts as an initiator that sets epigenetic marks. If the memory is lost, AP-1 is needed continuously to maintain it. Comparing the two timings separates these two mechanisms.

rewrites.title: Re-stimulation response assay with enhancer-level readouts
rewrites.description: Prime cells, rest them, then restimulate and measure faster or stronger transcription (nascent RNA-seq such as PRO-seq, or scRNA-seq) at AP-1-bound loci versus unprimed controls. Pair this with H3K27ac and chromatin accessibility profiling to link a heightened response to AP-1-marked enhancers, and test whether AP-1 binding site mutation (CRISPR) removes the effect.
